1.topic: Les salutations, les présentations, la date et le temps
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. greet people, introduce themselves and say goodbye in French, using tu and vous;
2. ask and answer questions about names, age and where they are from;
3. exchange information about days, dates and the weather.

## Materials

Name cards, a classroom calendar in French, weather picture cards, a short audio dialogue, the worksheet.

## Starter (7 minutes)

Greet students at the door: "Bonjour! Comment tu t'appelles?" Students answer "Je m'appelle ___." Write the exchange on the board. Point out that the apostrophe joins two words, and that the written accent marks are part of the spelling.

## Main activity

1. Greetings: bonjour (day), bonsoir (evening), salut (informal), and goodbyes: au revoir, à bientôt, à demain. Contrast tu (friends, classmates, family) with vous (adults you do not know, a teacher, more than one person): "Comment vas-tu?" versus "Comment allez-vous?"
2. Pair work: "Comment tu t'appelles? Quel âge as-tu? Tu es d'où?" Model answers: "Je m'appelle Léa. J'ai quinze ans. Je suis de Columbus." Notice that French uses avoir for age: "j'ai quinze ans," literally "I have fifteen years."
3. Days of the week (lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche), not capitalized, and dates: "Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi, le dix octobre." Weather with il fait: il fait froid, il fait chaud, il fait beau, il fait du vent; il pleut, il neige.
4. Record the weather in Columbus each morning on a class chart in French.

## Checking for understanding

Cold-call: "Quel temps fait-il aujourd'hui?" Listen for il fait + adjective and the correct use of tu and vous.

## Worksheet

A dialogue to complete and a weather chart.

reading.title: Bonjour, je m'appelle Léa
reading.content:
In French you greet people differently depending on the time of day and on how well you know them. In the morning and the afternoon you say **bonjour**. In the evening you say **bonsoir**. With friends, **salut** is common for both hello and goodbye. To say goodbye you can say **au revoir** (goodbye), **à bientôt** (see you soon), **à demain** (see you tomorrow) or **à lundi** (see you Monday).

French has two ways to say "you." With friends, classmates and family, use the informal **tu**: "Comment vas-tu?" (How are you?). With adults you do not know well, a teacher, or more than one person, use the formal **vous**: "Comment allez-vous?" Using the right form shows respect, and it is very important in France. Notice the accent marks. They are part of the spelling, and they change the sound: **é** (café), **è** (mère), **ê** (fête), **à** (à demain) and **ç** (français).

Read this short dialogue between two students at a high school in Columbus.

— Salut! Comment tu t'appelles?
— Je m'appelle Léa. Et toi?
— Moi, je m'appelle Marc. Enchanté!
— Enchantée. Quel âge as-tu, Marc?
— J'ai quinze ans. Et toi?
— J'ai quatorze ans. Je suis de Cleveland. Tu es d'où?
— Je suis de Columbus, mais ma famille est du Canada.

To say your age, French uses the verb **avoir** (to have): "J'ai quinze ans," literally "I have fifteen years." To say where you are from, use **être de**: "Je suis de l'Ohio."

You can also talk about the date and the weather. The days are **lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi** and **dimanche**, and they are not capitalized. A date puts the day first: "Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi, le dix octobre." For the weather, French uses the verb **faire**: "Il fait froid" (it is cold), "Il fait chaud" (it is hot), "Il fait beau" (the weather is nice), "Il fait du vent" (it is windy). For rain and snow there are special verbs: "Il pleut" (it rains) and "Il neige" (it snows). In Ohio in November you might say, "Aujourd'hui, il fait froid et il neige un peu."

2.topic: Décrire des personnes, l'école et ce qu'on a
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. describe people using être and adjectives that agree in gender and number;
2. talk about school, classes and supplies using avoir and il y a.

## Materials

Photos of famous people, picture cards of school supplies, a classroom with labeled objects, the quiz.

## Starter (6 minutes)

Hold up photos of a famous athlete and a singer. Ask in French: "Comment est-il? Comment est-elle?" Elicit adjectives and write them on the board: grand, grande, petit, petite, sympa, intelligent. Ask why some have an extra e.

## Main activity

1. Present être: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Describe people: "Mon amie est grande et sympa. Mon frère est grand et sympa." Discuss agreement: add -e for feminine and -s for plural (grands, grandes). Adjectives that already end in -e, like sympathique, do not change in the feminine.
2. Classes and supplies: la classe de maths, le français, l'anglais, les sciences, l'histoire, l'art; un stylo, un cahier, un sac à dos, une calculatrice, une règle. Articles: le, la, l', les, and un, une, des.
3. Avoir and il y a: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont; "J'ai un cahier. Il y a vingt élèves dans la classe."
4. Pair activity: "J'ai besoin d'un stylo. Tu as un stylo?"

## Checking for understanding

Whiteboard: write one sentence that describes your best friend with être and two adjectives.

## Quiz

Agreement, avoir and il y a.

reading.title: Mon amie Lucie et ma classe
reading.content:
In French, adjectives describe people and things, and they have to **agree** with the noun they describe. Most adjectives add **-e** for the feminine and **-s** for the plural: grand, grande, grands, grandes. An adjective that already ends in **-e**, such as **sympathique** or **jeune**, has the same form for masculine and feminine: un garçon sympathique, une fille sympathique. Some adjectives change a bit more: **intelligent** becomes **intelligente**, and **travailleur** becomes **travailleuse**. Adjectives usually go after the noun: "une fille intelligente," not "an intelligent girl" order.

To describe what someone is like we use the verb **être**: je **suis**, tu **es**, il/elle **est**, nous **sommes**, vous **êtes**, ils/elles **sont**. Read this paragraph about a Columbus student.

"Mon amie s'appelle Lucie. Elle est grande, mince et très sympa. Mon ami Paul est petit et travailleur. Lucie et Paul sont des élèves intelligents. Moi, je suis un peu timide, mais mes amis sont très amusants."

Now look at the classroom. The words for school things have a gender: **un** stylo, **un** cahier, **un** livre, **une** calculatrice, **une** chaise, **une** règle. To say "the," use **le**, **la**, **l'** (before a vowel) or **les**: le cahier, la chaise, l'élève, les livres. The school subjects are **les maths**, **le français**, **l'anglais**, **les sciences**, **l'histoire** and **l'art**, and a class is **un cours** or **la classe de maths**.

Two verbs help us talk about what we have. **Avoir** means "to have": j'**ai**, tu **as**, il/elle **a**, nous **avons**, vous **avez**, ils/elles **ont**. "J'ai six cours. Mon ami a une calculatrice." The expression **il y a** means both "there is" and "there are," and it never changes: "Il y a vingt-cinq élèves dans la classe." "Il y a un cahier sur la table." "Il n'y a pas de stylos."

To say what you need, use **avoir besoin de**: "J'ai besoin d'un stylo et d'un cahier." To ask a classmate, say: "Tu as un stylo?" Notice how often we use avoir with school things, with an article that matches the noun.

3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. say what they like and do not like with aimer and préférer;
2. tell time and say when classes begin and end.

## Materials

A paper clock for each pair, picture cards of activities, a class schedule template, the problem set.

## Starter (6 minutes)

Hold up pictures: a pizza, a basketball, homework. Ask in French: "Tu aimes la pizza?" Students answer "Oui, j'aime" or "Non, je n'aime pas." Draw a thumbs up and down.

## Main activity

1. Aimer and préférer: j'aime, tu aimes, il aime, nous aimons, vous aimez, ils aiment. Je préfère (note the accent change). Use the definite article for general likes: "J'aime la musique. J'aime les sports. Je préfère le basket." With an infinitive: "J'aime danser." Negative: je n'aime pas.
2. Interview: students ask three classmates "Tu aimes le basket? Tu préfères les maths ou l'histoire?" and record answers.
3. Time: Quelle heure est-il? Il est une heure. Il est deux heures. Il est trois heures et quart, et demie, moins le quart. Midi, minuit. À quelle heure est la classe? À huit heures. Add du matin, de l'après-midi, du soir.
4. Make a short schedule of four classes with times.

## Checking for understanding

Show the paper clock: 8:15, 9:30, 12:45. Students say the time in French.

## Problem set

Likes and time.

reading.title: Qu'est-ce que tu aimes? Quelle heure est-il?
reading.content:
To say you like something in French, use the verb **aimer** (to like, to love). It is a regular **-er** verb: j'**aime**, tu **aimes**, il/elle **aime**, nous **aimons**, vous **aimez**, ils/elles **aiment**. Before a vowel, **je** becomes **j'**. When you talk about what you like in general, French uses the definite article, which English does not: "J'aime **la** musique. J'aime **les** sports. J'aime **le** chocolat." You can also like an activity by using the infinitive: "J'aime danser. J'aime jouer au basket." To say you prefer, use **préférer**: "Je préfère le football." Notice the accent marks change in the pronunciation: je préfère, nous préférons. To say you do not like something, put **ne** before the verb and **pas** after it: "Je **n'**aime **pas** les devoirs."

To ask a classmate, say: "Tu aimes le basket?" or "Tu préfères les maths ou l'histoire?" The answer can be "Oui, j'aime ça" or "Non, je n'aime pas ça."

Look at a sample interview.

— Tu aimes le cours de sciences?
— Oui, j'aime beaucoup ça. J'adore les expériences. Et toi?
— Moi, je n'aime pas les sciences, mais j'aime l'art.

To tell time, use **il est**. "Quelle heure est-il?" "Il est une heure." "Il est deux heures." For minutes, add **et** (past) or **moins** (to): "Il est trois heures dix." "Il est quatre heures **et quart**" (4:15). "Il est cinq heures **et demie**" (5:30). "Il est six heures **moins le quart**" (5:45). Noon is **midi** and midnight is **minuit**. To say when something happens, use **à**: "Le cours de français est à neuf heures et demie." To say AM or PM, add **du matin**, **de l'après-midi** or **du soir**: "Mon premier cours commence à huit heures du matin et le dernier finit à trois heures de l'après-midi."

In an American high school many students start at about 7:30 or 8:00 and finish in the early afternoon. Here is a short schedule: "J'ai le cours d'anglais à huit heures, le cours de maths à neuf heures, le déjeuner à midi et le cours d'art à une heure."

4.topic: Les verbes en -er et les sons du français
4.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. use regular -er verbs in the present tense to say what people do;
2. recognize French sounds, accents and liaison, and read simple words aloud.

## Materials

Audio of the French alphabet and minimal pairs, a verb conjugation chart, picture cards of activities, a class poster of the accents, the worksheet.

## Starter (6 minutes)

Read aloud the words rue, route, vous, tu, dessous and ask students to say what they notice about u versus ou. Introduce the idea that French letters and sounds do not always match English, and that listening is a skill.

## Main activity

1. Present regular -er verbs: parler, étudier, danser, chanter, travailler, écouter, regarder, manger. Remove -er and add endings: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Examples: je parle français, tu étudies beaucoup, elle danse bien, nous mangeons à midi (the e before -ons keeps the soft g), ils travaillent dans un restaurant.
2. Pronunciation: most final consonants are silent (petit, vous); accents (é, è, ê, à, ç); the nasal vowels (bon, un, an); the French r; liaison: les amis [lez-ami], vous avez [vou-z-avé]. Silent h.
3. Pair activity: each partner says three things they do on a school day and the other writes what they heard.

## Checking for understanding

Whiteboards: conjugate "étudier" for je, tu, elle, nous. Spell your name aloud in French.

## Worksheet

Conjugation and a pronunciation exercise.

reading.title: Ce que nous faisons tous les jours
reading.content:
Most French verbs end in **-er** in their basic form, called the infinitive. This week we learn the regular **-er** verbs. To use one in the present tense, drop the **-er** and add an ending that shows who is doing the action. For **parler** (to speak) the forms are:

- je **parle**
- tu **parles**
- il / elle / on **parle**
- nous **parlons**
- vous **parlez**
- ils / elles **parlent**

Other common regular -er verbs are **étudier** (to study), **danser** (to dance), **chanter** (to sing), **travailler** (to work), **écouter** (to listen to), **regarder** (to watch), **manger** (to eat) and **jouer** (to play). They follow the same pattern. Because the ending is not always pronounced (parle, parles and parlent all sound the same), the subject pronoun is always needed in French. There is no separate form for "I am studying," so "j'étudie" can mean "I study" or "I am studying." Before a vowel, **je** becomes **j'**: j'étudie, j'écoute. With **manger**, the nous form adds an **e** to keep the soft sound: nous mangeons.

Here are some examples. "Je parle anglais et un peu de français." "Tu étudies avec tes amis." "Ma sœur chante dans la chorale de l'école." "Nous écoutons de la musique le matin." "Mes parents travaillent dans un hôpital." To make a sentence negative, put **ne** before the verb and **pas** after it: "Je ne parle pas espagnol."

French pronunciation is different from English. Many final consonants are **silent**: in "petit" the t is not pronounced, and in "vous" the s is silent. The **accent marks** change the sound or distinguish words: **é** is like "ay," **è** and **ê** are like "eh," and **ç** is a soft "s." The letters **u** and **ou** are different: "tu" has rounded lips, and "vous" sounds like "oo." The **nasal vowels** (bon, un, an) are pronounced partly through the nose. The **r** is made at the back of the throat. **Liaison** means that a normally silent final consonant is pronounced when the next word begins with a vowel: "les amis" sounds like "lay-zah-mee," and "vous avez" sounds like "voo-zah-vay." The letter **h** is silent. Practice by listening and repeating, and notice how syllables are spoken with an even rhythm, without a strong stress on one syllable.

5.topic: Les nombres, la famille et l'idée principale
5.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. understand numbers from 0 to 100 and use them for ages, prices and phone numbers;
2. find the main idea in a short text about a French school;
3. present information about themselves and their family in a short spoken or written description.

## Materials

Number cards, play money, a menu with prices from a crêperie, a short text about a French school day, the worksheet.

## Starter (6 minutes)

Play "bingo" with numbers from 1 to 50. Call numbers in French and students mark them. Review 1 to 20 first, then 21 to 29 (vingt et un, vingt-deux), then the tens.

## Main activity

1. Numbers: 0 to 20; 21 (vingt et un), 22 to 29; 30 trente, 40 quarante, 50 cinquante, 60 soixante; then 70 (soixante-dix), 80 (quatre-vingts), 90 (quatre-vingt-dix), 100 cent. Use them for ages, phone numbers (read in pairs of digits), and prices: "La crêpe coûte six euros cinquante."
2. Family vocabulary: ma mère, mon père, mon frère, ma sœur, mes grands-parents, mon oncle, ma cousine. Possessives mon / ma / mes, ton / ta / tes, son / sa / ses.
3. Reading for the main idea: students read a short paragraph about a French lycée (students stay in a classroom, the school day may end at 5:00, a long lunch at the cantine, no sports teams in the school). Strategies: look for cognates, repeated words and the first sentence.
4. Presentation: prepare a 40-second description of your family: names, ages and one thing each person does.

## Checking for understanding

Whiteboards: write the number your teacher says, and a price.

## Worksheet

Numbers, family vocabulary and a main-idea reading.

reading.title: Ma famille et les nombres
reading.content:
Learning the numbers in French is useful every day. From 0 to 20 you learn each word: **zéro, un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize, dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt**. From 21 to 29 the words are built: **vingt et un, vingt-deux, vingt-trois**. For the tens, learn **trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante** and then the special ones: **soixante-dix** (70, literally sixty-ten), **quatre-vingts** (80, literally four twenties), **quatre-vingt-dix** (90) and **cent** (100). From 31 on, put them together with **et** for numbers ending in one, and a hyphen for the others: trente et un (31), quarante-cinq (45), quatre-vingt-dix-neuf (99). We use numbers for ages, as in "Mon grand-père a soixante-dix-huit ans." For prices: "Une crêpe coûte six euros." For phone numbers, French speakers say two digits at a time: 06 12 34 56 78 is "zéro six, douze, trente-quatre, cinquante-six, soixante-dix-huit."

Family words are also important. **Ma mère** and **mon père** are your parents. **Mon frère** and **ma sœur** are your brother and sister. **Mes grands-parents** are your grandparents. **Mon oncle** and **ma tante** are an uncle and an aunt; **mon cousin** and **ma cousine** are a male or female cousin. To show possession, use **mon / ma / mes** (my), **ton / ta / tes** (your) and **son / sa / ses** (his, her). The word changes with the noun: mon frère, ma sœur, mes parents. Before a vowel use **mon** even for a feminine noun: mon amie.

Reading in a new language is easier if you look for the **main idea**, not every word. Look at the title, the first sentence, the words that repeat and words that look like English words (cognates). Read this short text.

"Je m'appelle Camille et j'ai seize ans. Je suis élève dans un lycée à Lyon. Le lycée est grand et il y a mille élèves. Les cours commencent à huit heures et finissent à cinq heures. À midi, nous mangeons à la cantine avec nos amis, et le repas est long. Mon cours préféré est le cours d'histoire."

What is the main idea? The text is about Camille's school day in France. A good title would be "La journée de Camille au lycée." You do not need to understand every word, such as "cantine" (cafeteria) or "finissent" (end), to know the main idea.

To present your own family, first say who you are, then name each person, say their age and what they do. "Ma famille est petite. J'ai un frère, Jack. Il a douze ans. Il aime jouer au foot."

6.topic: Mon emploi du temps et la bise
6.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. write a short paragraph about their schedule and favorite subjects;
2. compare greetings, such as la bise and the handshake, in France and the French-speaking world.

## Materials

A sample schedule in French, short video clips of greetings in France, Québec and Senegal, a writing rubric, the worksheet.

## Starter (6 minutes)

Show two photos: a handshake at a business meeting in Columbus, and two friends greeting with a kiss on each cheek in Paris. Ask in English: "What differences do you see?" Record ideas.

## Main activity

1. Model a paragraph: "Ma journée à l'école." Include time, classes, a verb in the present tense, and an opinion. Use connecting words: d'abord, ensuite, aussi, mais, parce que.
2. Students write their own paragraph of five to six sentences, using the schedule from last week and at least three -er verbs and aimer.
3. Greetings across cultures: in France friends and family greet with la bise, kisses on the cheek (two in Paris, but the number varies by region from one to four), people shake hands in formal situations, and the use of vous shows respect. In Québec and in Senegal, customs differ again. Discuss that customs vary by country, region and family.
4. Make a Venn diagram comparing greetings in the French-speaking world and in the US.

## Checking for understanding

Ask: "When would you use vous instead of tu, and how does that show respect?"

## Worksheet

Questions about the paragraph and the cultural comparison.

reading.title: Mon emploi du temps et comment on se dit bonjour
reading.content:
Writing a paragraph in French means connecting short sentences with simple linking words. Useful words are **d'abord** (first), **ensuite** (then, next), **aussi** (also), **mais** (but), **parce que** (because) and **et** (and). A paragraph about your schedule might include the time, the class, a verb in the present tense and an opinion. Read this model.

"Ma journée à l'école est longue, mais j'aime ça. D'abord, j'ai le cours d'anglais à huit heures du matin. Ensuite, j'étudie les maths à neuf heures et demie. Mon cours préféré est le cours d'art parce que j'aime dessiner. J'aime aussi le cours de français parce que la prof est très sympa. L'après-midi, mes amis et moi, nous marchons à la maison et nous écoutons de la musique."

Notice that the paragraph uses **j'aime**, regular -er verbs (étudie, dessiner, marchons, écoutons), and times (à huit heures du matin). It also begins with a topic sentence that gives the main idea, and each next sentence adds a detail.

Language is only one part of communicating. Greetings and personal space differ from one culture to another. In the United States, a handshake is common in formal situations, and friends often greet with a wave or a short hug. In France, friends and family usually greet each other with **la bise**, a light kiss on each cheek. In Paris it is usually two kisses, but in other regions the number can be one, three or four. Women often greet both women and men this way, while men often shake hands or give the bise to relatives and close friends. In formal situations, with an adult you do not know, people shake hands and use **vous**. It is polite to say **bonjour** when you enter a shop, even before you ask for anything, and to say **au revoir** when you leave. People in France often stand closer to each other than most Americans do.

In Québec, many people also use the bise with friends, while in Senegal, greetings can be long and warm, with several questions about family and health, and handshakes are common. These are general customs. They differ by country, by region and by family, and many people who live in the United States mix traditions. The best way to be respectful is to observe what others do and to ask politely.

reading.title: Deux traditions et une carte
reading.content:
French is spoken by more than 300 million people on five continents, and each region has its own traditions. This week we learn about two celebrations, a few products, and the map of the French-speaking world.

**La Fête nationale** is celebrated in France on July 14. It remembers the day in 1789 when people stormed the Bastille, a prison in Paris, an event that became a symbol of the French Revolution. Today there are parades, concerts and fireworks, and the biggest military parade goes down the Champs-Élysées in Paris. Families and friends gather in the evening for picnics and fireworks, and many towns hold a dance, le bal des pompiers. The holiday is also celebrated by French communities in the United States, including in Columbus, where cultural associations organize events.

**La galette des rois** is a cake eaten around January 6, the Epiphany. In northern France it is a round, flaky pastry filled with almond cream. Inside is hidden a small figure, **la fève**. The youngest person at the table goes under the table and says who gets each slice. The person who finds the fève becomes king or queen for the day and wears a paper crown. Another tradition is **la Chandeleur** on February 2, when families eat **crêpes**. It is said that if you hold a coin in one hand and flip a crêpe in the pan with the other, you will have luck and money all year.

French products are also well known: **la baguette**, the long bread that many people buy fresh every day at the **boulangerie**; **le fromage**, with hundreds of varieties; **les macarons**; and **le parfum**, made in the region of Grasse.

Knowing where French is spoken helps us understand the world. The country names and capitals include: **la France** (capital: Paris), **le Canada** (Ottawa), **la Belgique** (Bruxelles), **la Suisse** (Berne), **le Sénégal** (Dakar), **le Mali** (Bamako), **la Côte d'Ivoire** (Yamoussoukro), **le Maroc** (Rabat), **Haïti** (Port-au-Prince) and **Madagascar** (Antananarivo). To ask a question, use "Quelle est la capitale du Sénégal?" and answer "La capitale du Sénégal est Dakar." Notice that country names have an article: **le** Canada, **la** France, **les** États-Unis. French is also an official language in many other countries and territories, including Luxembourg, Cameroun, Tunisie and Polynésie française.

8.topic: Les mots amis, les faux amis et le français autour de nous
8.lessonNote:
## Objectives

Students will be able to:

1. notice similarities between French and English words, including cognates;
2. find examples of French in their community, such as products and signs, and report what they say.

## Materials

A list of cognates and false friends, photos of French on products and signs (cereal boxes, perfume, a bakery, Canadian labels), a class scavenger hunt sheet, the problem set.

## Starter (6 minutes)

Write on the board: important, restaurant, université, banane, orange. Ask in English: "Can you guess what these mean?" Introduce the word "cognate" and show that many French words look like English because English borrowed a lot of its vocabulary from French after 1066.

## Main activity

1. Cognates: common endings -tion = -tion (information, nation), -ité = -ity (université, qualité), -eux = -ous (délicieux), -ment = -ly (finalement). Cognates help in reading, but pronunciation differs.
2. False friends (faux amis): une librairie is a bookstore, not a library (une bibliothèque); actuellement means currently; assister à means to attend; sensible means sensitive; une location is a rental; le pain is bread, not pain; and rester means to stay. Discuss how to check meaning in context.
3. French around us: students examine real examples (a cereal box with French on the back, a perfume bottle, a bakery sign, a menu with croissant and crêpe) and report in English what each says, and in French one word they recognize.
4. Homework: find one example of French in your community and write a short report.

## Checking for understanding

Ask: "If you read 'La librairie est dans la rue Main,' what is the building and what is it not?"

## Problem set

Cognates, false friends and a community example.

reading.title: Des mots amis et des mots traîtres
reading.content:
One of the best things about learning French as an English speaker is that thousands of words look and mean almost the same in both languages. These words are called **cognates**, and there are so many because after the Norman conquest of England in 1066, French was the language of the English court for about three centuries, and English took in thousands of French words. Examples are **important**, **famille**, **restaurant**, **animal**, **musique**, **chocolat** and **orange**. There are patterns that help you find more. English words ending in **-tion** often match French exactly: *information* is *information*, *nation* is *nation*. English **-ity** becomes **-ité**: *university* is *université*, *quality* is *qualité*. English **-ous** becomes **-eux**: *delicious* is *délicieux*. English **-ly** adverbs often match **-ment**: *finally* is *finalement*. Cognates help you understand new texts quickly. Remember that they are pronounced in a French way, and the spelling may differ slightly: *restaurant* is "res-toh-RAHN."

Not all similar words are friends. A **false friend** (faux ami) looks like an English word but has a different meaning. A **librairie** is a bookstore, not a library, which is a **bibliothèque**. The word **actuellement** means "currently," not "actually," which is **en fait**. **Assister à** means "to attend," not "to assist," which is **aider**. **Sensible** means "sensitive," not "sensible," which is **raisonnable**. A **location** is a rental, not a place, which is **un endroit**. **Rester** means "to stay," not "to rest," which is **se reposer**. When a word seems strange in context, use the other words in the sentence to decide. If "J'assiste au cours de maths" comes from a student, "attend" makes sense and "assist" does not.

French is also all around you. On the back of many cereal boxes and food packages in the United States you can see French, because the same package is sold in Canada, where the law requires both English and French. On a package, **ingrédients**, **valeur nutritive**, **sans sucre ajouté** (no added sugar) and **à conserver au réfrigérateur** (keep refrigerated) are French you can read with cognates. Perfumes and fashion brands use French names, bakery signs say **boulangerie** and **pâtisserie**, and menus offer **croissants**, **crêpes** and **soupe à l'oignon**. In Columbus and Ohio you might also meet French speakers from Canada, Haiti, West Africa and France. When you find an example, you can report what it says, where you saw it, and who you think it is for. Doing so shows how the language is part of everyday life and not just a school subject.
